HCM is the most common inherited cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. It is characterised by a dominant mutation in sarcomeric proteins, such as myosin or actin. Histological evaluation reveals myocyte disarray, where myocytes are not oriented in parallel, and often hypertrophy of the interventricular septum. HCM can present with outflow tract obstruction, arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death. HCM can be managed with beta-blockers and if the patient is at high risk of sudden cardiac death, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) may be implanted.

Lynch Syndrome is associated with colorectal cancer, and has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Therefore, if Ashton has Lynch syndrome, he would have inherited a mutated copy of a mismatch repair gene from either his mother or his father.  Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is associated with a germline mutation in the APC gene. This results in hundreds of polyps forming in the colon, and colorectal cancer developing in most patients by the age of 40.  Brunner's Adenomatous Polyps are associated with a germline mutation in the MYH gene. These are multiple polyps that form in the colon, and usually don't lead to colorectal cancer.  Note that while the APC gene is a mismatch repair gene, a germline mutation in the APC gene causes FAP, whereas mismatch repair gene mutations cause Lynch syndrome.  Source: Kumar and Clark

Sentinel cells are a type of cell that act as the first line of defence against infection. They are cells that are constantly monitoring the environment for signs of infection, and if detected, they will activate an inflammatory response.  They are all nucleated cells, and can be found in different tissues.  Spleen  Kidney  Lung  Brain (microglial cells)  Skin (Langerhans cells)  Blood (dendritic cells and macrophages)  Intestine (dendritic cells and macrophages)  Uterus (macrophages)  Mouth (dendritic cells)  Other (dendritic cells and macrophages)  Note that some tissues contain more sentinel cells than others.  Natural killer cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes that are part of the adaptive immune system. They are not sentinel cells because they do not act as the first line of defence. Instead, they act as an important part of the second line of defence, killing virally infected cells that have been identified by the adaptive immune system as infected.

HCN4 channels are hyperpolarised cyclic gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels. Activation by noradrenaline causes depolarisation and a slower repolarisation phase. This increases the sinoatrial node firing rate (Chronotropy). Ryanodine receptors are the receptors activated by increased Ca2+ levels in the cytosol that open calcium release channels on the SR. This causes more Ca2+ to be released and therefore more forceful contractions (Inotropy). It also shortens the time between contractions (Lucitropy).

Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption, potassium secretion and it also stimulates the release of ADH from the posterior pituitary gland. ADH increases water reabsorption by the kidneys.  Increased sodium reabsorption can be followed by water absorption down the osmotic gradient, therefore increasing blood volume.  This is important in salt wasting states such as Conn's syndrome.

Monoamine oxidase inhibitors prevent the breakdown of tyramine, which is found in foods such as cheese. This leads to excess tyramine, which causes a rapid release of catecholamines, resulting in a hypertensive crisis.

Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT I) is an enzyme found on the outer mitochondrial membrane. It catalyses the reaction of an Acyl-CoA molecule with carnitine, to form Acylcarnitine. Acylcarnitine can then be transported across the mitochondrial membrane via the carrier protein Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. Carnitine acyltransferase II (CAT II) is found on the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyses the reverse reaction, converting Acylcarnitine back into Acyl-CoA and carnitine. Acyl-CoA is then available for beta-oxidation.  Enolase is an enzyme used in glycolysis. Acyl-CoA synthetase is an enzyme used in the activation of fatty acids.

Calsequestrin and FKBP inhibit the Ryanodine receptor which is found on the SR. When calcium levels rise, these inhibitors are outcompeted allowing the channel to open and release more calcium from the SR.  PKA and cAMP stimulate contractility by phosphorylating and activating phospholamban which in turn removes the inhibition of the SERCA pump. This causes more calcium to be actively taken up into the SR so that more can be released.  Calbindin is found on the rough ER and binds calcium to prevent it crystallising.  Sodium and calcium ions are just ions.

Agranulocytosis is a severe form of neutropenia characterised by the near total absence of granulocytes in the blood. Clozapine is known to cause agranulocytosis, which is an idiosyncratic reaction and is dose independent. The classic presentation of agranulocytosis is the development of a febrile illness with minor infections (e.g. gingivitis, angular stomatitis) preceding the onset of high fever and potentially leading to septicaemia.
